title: Content-Security-Policy img-src allows plaintext HTTP sources
description: The Content-Security-Policy img-src directive lists the scheme source `http:`, either alone or beside other sources, so the browser may load images over plaintext HTTP. A network attacker who can answer that request supplies the images himself, and the response that carries the policy is not the response that decides what loads.
remediation: Remove `http:` from img-src and name the exact HTTPS origins that are needed. If a legacy origin still serves over HTTP, terminate TLS in front of it and list the HTTPS name instead of relaxing the directive.
limitation: One header value and one directive. The rule reports the scheme token in img-src only; when img-src is absent the default-src fallback decides, and other rules report that case. It cannot tell whether the plaintext origin is reachable from the browser that receives the policy.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy carries an explicit img-src directive whose source list contains the `http:` scheme token.
fp: A deployment that deliberately proxies a legacy plaintext origin is still flagged; the finding is the scheme in the policy, not proof that the origin answers the browser.
recordDesc: The img-src directive permits plaintext HTTP images, so a network attacker can substitute image content and read the request path that carries page data.
applicability: Responses that send Content-Security-Policy with an explicit img-src directive.
risk: Images load over plaintext: the attacker on the path replaces the pixels and learns what the page asked for; MEDIUM because the channel needs the plaintext hop to exist.
why: img-src carries the `http:` scheme source.
fix: Remove the http: token from img-src.
Re-read img-src and confirm every remaining source is https or a keyword.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and read the img-src directive; no source may carry the http: scheme.

title: Content-Security-Policy script-src allows unsafe-hashes
description: The Content-Security-Policy script-src directive lists the `'unsafe-hashes'` keyword, which re-enables inline event-handler attributes and `javascript:` URLs whenever their body matches a hash in the same policy. A policy that otherwise looks nonce-based therefore still accepts a set of inline handlers written into the markup.
remediation: Remove `'unsafe-hashes'` and move the handler bodies into nonce-approved script blocks. Where a legacy handler must stay, rewrite it as an addEventListener call in an external script that the policy already allows.
limitation: One header value and one directive. The rule reports the keyword in script-src; it does not evaluate whether the policy also lists a hash that matches a handler in the page, because that comparison needs the document body and the policy together.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy script-src directive contains the `'unsafe-hashes'` keyword.
fp: A policy that lists hashes no handler matches is still flagged; the finding is the keyword, not proof that a matching handler exists in the document.
recordDesc: `'unsafe-hashes'` lets an injected inline handler run when its text matches a hash the policy lists, so the policy is not the nonce-only barrier that its other keywords suggest.
applicability: Responses that send Content-Security-Policy with an explicit script-src directive.
risk: Inline handlers that match a listed hash execute in the page origin despite the nonce-based policy; MEDIUM because the attacker must reuse handler text the policy already trusts.
why: script-src contains the `'unsafe-hashes'` keyword.
fix: Remove 'unsafe-hashes' from script-src.
Move the inline handler bodies into nonce-approved script.
verifyT: Fetch the page and read script-src; the keyword must be absent and the remaining handlers must be bound from an allowed script.

title: Content-Security-Policy script-src allows wasm-unsafe-eval
description: The Content-Security-Policy script-src directive lists `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, which re-enables WebAssembly compilation in a policy that otherwise forbids evaluation. WebAssembly modules can implement behaviour the policy's JavaScript restrictions do not express, and the keyword is often added to unblock one dependency.
remediation: Remove `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` unless the page genuinely needs WebAssembly, and keep `'unsafe-eval'` absent. If a single module is required, pin the script source that delivers it and document the exception.
limitation: One header value and one directive. The rule reports the keyword in script-src; it does not inspect which module the page loads or whether compilation is reachable from an injection point.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy script-src directive contains the `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` keyword.
fp: The keyword permits compilation; the rule does not prove that any WebAssembly module is served or reachable.
recordDesc: `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` re-enables WebAssembly compilation, so a module delivered through an allowed script source can execute logic the JavaScript policy was meant to constrain.
applicability: Responses that send Content-Security-Policy with an explicit script-src directive.
risk: A compromised allowed script source ships a WebAssembly module and runs its logic in the page origin; MEDIUM because the module still has to arrive through an allowed script source.
why: script-src contains the `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` keyword.
fix: Remove 'wasm-unsafe-eval' from script-src.
Confirm the page still works without WebAssembly, or pin the one source that needs it.
verifyT: Fetch the page and read script-src; the keyword must be gone unless a documented module needs it.

title: Content-Security-Policy default-src allows data: URLs
description: The Content-Security-Policy default-src directive lists the `data:` scheme, so every resource class without a directive of its own may load a data: URL. When script-src is absent the fallback reaches scripts as well, and a data: script URL is an inline-script carrier that needs no network origin.
remediation: Remove `data:` from default-src and name the classes that genuinely need it, such as img-src, in their own directive. Keep script-src and object-src explicit so the fallback cannot reach them.
limitation: One header value and one directive. The rule reports `data:` in default-src; it does not compute which class is actually governed by the fallback in a given policy, because that depends on which other directives are present.
scopeT: One response whose Content-Security-Policy default-src directive contains the `data:` scheme token.
fp: A policy that also sets script-src to 'none' is still flagged; the finding is the fallback scheme, not proof that a data: script is reachable.
recordDesc: `data:` in default-src is inherited by every directive without an explicit value, so inline data URLs become an allowed resource source for scripts, frames and styles alike.
applicability: Responses that send Content-Security-Policy with an explicit default-src directive.
risk: Injected markup points a fallback-governed directive at a data: URL and the payload executes or renders without any external origin; MEDIUM because explicit directives shield the classes they name.
why: default-src contains the `data:` scheme token.
fix: Remove data: from default-src.
List data: only in the specific directive that needs it, such as img-src.
verifyT: Fetch the page and read default-src; the data: token must be gone and any data URL use must be named per directive.

title: Set-Cookie Max-Age is not a valid integer
description: The Set-Cookie header carries a Max-Age attribute whose value is not a run of digits, so a user agent ignores the attribute entirely. The cookie then falls back to the Expires attribute or to session lifetime, which is rarely what the deployment intended and silently changes how long the credential survives.
remediation: Write Max-Age as a decimal number of seconds. If both Max-Age and Expires are sent, make them agree so no user agent has to choose between them.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the attribute token and never decides whether the cookie is a session cookie; a browser that ignores the attribute applies its own fallback, which the observation cannot show.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie header whose Max-Age attribute value is not a run of digits.
fp: A malformed Max-Age is still flagged when Expires carries the intended lifetime; the finding is the unparsable attribute, not a specific expiry date.
recordDesc: A Max-Age value a user agent cannot parse is discarded, so the cookie persists for a different lifetime than the header appears to declare.
applicability: Responses that set a cookie with a Max-Age attribute.
risk: A credential outlives the window the deployment meant to set, or dies at browser close when persistence was intended; LOW because the effect is a lifetime mismatch rather than direct exposure.
why: Max-Age is present with a value that is not a run of digits.
fix: Rewrite Max-Age as decimal seconds.
Confirm Max-Age and Expires agree where both are sent.
verifyT: Re-read Set-Cookie and confirm every Max-Age value is a decimal integer.

title: Set-Cookie declares SameSite more than once
description: The Set-Cookie header contains two SameSite attributes. RFC 6265 defines last-wins behaviour for an attribute that repeats, but intermediaries and older user agents have disagreed, and the header itself no longer states one unambiguous policy. A cookie that reads as Lax to one parser can be None to another.
remediation: Emit exactly one SameSite attribute per cookie. If a framework contributes one, remove the hand-written copy rather than appending a second.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the repeated attribute and does not decide which value wins, because that depends on the user agent; the effective protection is outside the observation.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie header whose attribute list contains the SameSite name twice.
fp: A duplicate with identical values is still flagged; the finding is the ambiguous header, not a specific effective policy.
recordDesc: Two SameSite attributes in one header make the effective policy parser-dependent, so the protection the deployment believes it set is not the only reading of the header.
applicability: Responses that set a cookie with a SameSite attribute.
risk: A parser that honours the first attribute keeps a stricter policy than the deployment intends, or a looser one, depending on the order; LOW because the common user agents agree on last-wins.
why: The SameSite attribute name appears twice in one Set-Cookie value.
fix: Emit a single SameSite attribute.
Check the framework configuration that adds the attribute by default.
verifyT: Re-read Set-Cookie and confirm each cookie carries one SameSite attribute.

title: Set-Cookie Path attribute is not absolute
description: The Set-Cookie header carries a Path attribute that does not begin with `/`, so a user agent ignores the value and derives the default path from the request URL instead. The cookie is then sent to a path scope the deployment did not choose, which is usually wider than the one written in the header.
remediation: Write Path with a leading slash, normally `Path=/`, and scope it to the narrowest directory that needs the cookie.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the attribute against its grammar and does not compute the default path a particular browser would derive from the request URL.
scopeT: One Set-Cookie header whose Path attribute value does not begin with a slash.
fp: An empty Path value is reported too, and a browser that ignores the attribute is not distinguished from one that stores the default path.
recordDesc: A relative Path value is discarded by the user agent, which falls back to the default-path algorithm and may send the cookie to more of the site than the header names.
applicability: Responses that set a cookie with a Path attribute.
risk: The cookie is attached to requests outside the intended directory, which widens the surface that can read or overwrite it; LOW because the default path is still scoped to the request directory tree.
why: Path is present and its value does not begin with a slash.
fix: Write Path with a leading slash.
Narrow the path to the directory that needs the cookie.
verifyT: Re-read Set-Cookie and confirm Path begins with a slash.

title: Secure cookie attribute delivered over plaintext HTTP
description: A response fetched over plaintext HTTP sets a cookie with the Secure attribute. The attribute asks the user agent to send the cookie only over TLS, but the header that delivered it already crossed the network unprotected, and several user agents refuse to store a Secure cookie that arrived over an insecure origin at all.
remediation: Serve the endpoint over HTTPS and mark the cookie Secure there. Redirect plaintext requests to HTTPS before any Set-Cookie is emitted rather than issuing the cookie on the plaintext response.
limitation: One header value and the scheme of the observation URL. The rule judges a Secure attribute on an http response only; over https the same header is correct and is not reported.
scopeT: One http response whose Set-Cookie header carries the Secure attribute.
fp: A plaintext redirect that sets no cookie is not reported; the rule needs the attribute in the same response.
recordDesc: A Secure attribute on a cookie delivered over plaintext protects nothing at the moment of delivery: the value is already on the wire, and the user agent may discard it as an insecure-origin set.
applicability: Plaintext HTTP responses that set a cookie with the Secure attribute.
risk: The cookie value is readable by anyone on the path while the attributes suggest it is protected, and the session may silently fail to persist; MEDIUM because the exposure happens on every plaintext response that sets it.
why: A Set-Cookie carrying Secure arrives over http.
fix: Serve the endpoint over HTTPS.
Issue Set-Cookie only on the TLS response.
verifyT: Request the http URL and confirm it redirects before any Set-Cookie is emitted; request the https URL and confirm the cookie is untouched.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin names more than one origin
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin value contains two origins, separated by whitespace or a comma. The CORS protocol allows exactly one origin or the literal `*`; a list never matches the requesting origin, so the grant the deployment intended silently fails and the header records a confusion about how the value is consumed.
remediation: Emit one origin per response, chosen from the request's Origin against an explicit allow-list. Never concatenate several origins into one header value.
limitation: One header value. The rule reads the declared value and cannot see the request Origin, so it cannot tell which of the listed origins was intended for this response.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin value contains two origin tokens.
fp: A header that lists one origin is not reported; the rule needs the second token in the same value.
recordDesc: A multi-origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin is never a valid grant, so browsers reject it and the intended cross-origin access stops working while the header still looks permissive.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
risk: Cross-origin clients fail closed in the browser while non-browser consumers of the header may read it as an allow-list; LOW because the browser outcome is denial rather than exposure.
why: The value contains two origin tokens.
fix: Emit a single origin chosen from an allow-list.
Remove any code that joins several origins with a space or comma.
verifyT: Request the endpoint with two different Origin values and confirm exactly one origin is returned each time.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin carries no host
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin value is a scheme with no host, such as `https://`. An origin is scheme, host and port; a scheme alone can never equal a requesting origin, so the header grants nothing while it reads like a deliberate wildcard.
remediation: Replace the bare scheme with the exact origin the client uses, including any non-default port, or with the literal `*` if the resource really is public.
limitation: One header value. The rule judges the declared value and cannot see which origin asked, so it does not claim the response was ever usable.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin value is a scheme with no host component.
fp: A value of `*` is not reported here; the wildcard has its own rule and a different meaning.
recordDesc: A scheme-only Access-Control-Allow-Origin matches no origin, so the intended cross-origin access silently fails and the value hides which client was meant to be allowed.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
risk: The browser denies the cross-origin read while an operator reading the header may believe a broad grant exists; LOW because the failure is closed.
why: The value is a scheme with optional slashes and nothing else.
fix: Replace the bare scheme with an exact origin.
Use the literal * only for genuinely public resources.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and confirm the returned value names a host, or is exactly *.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin carries userinfo
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin value contains a `user@host` form. An origin has no userinfo component, so the value can never match the requesting origin; it also suggests the value was assembled from an untrusted URL rather than from a fixed allow-list.
remediation: Compare a parsed origin object against an allow-list and emit `origin.scheme://origin.host[:port]`. Never copy a URL string into the header.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the userinfo form and cannot see whether the value was derived from the request Origin.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Origin value carries a userinfo component.
fp: A path that contains `@` after the first slash is not reported; only userinfo before the host counts.
recordDesc: A userinfo-bearing Access-Control-Allow-Origin never matches an origin, so the grant fails while the header shows that a URL string, not a parsed origin, is being reflected.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
risk: The browser denies the read, and the header records that an unparsed URL reached it; LOW because the outcome is a failed grant rather than exposure.
why: The value carries an `@` between the scheme and the first slash.
fix: Emit a parsed origin without userinfo.
Stop reflecting raw URL strings into the header.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and confirm the returned value has no @ component.

title: Access-Control-Max-Age is not a delta-seconds value
description: The Access-Control-Max-Age value is not a run of digits, so a browser ignores it and falls back to its own default preflight cache lifetime. The deployment's intention to cache the preflight for a chosen period is not honoured, and the observable configuration no longer matches the documented one.
remediation: Write Access-Control-Max-Age as decimal seconds. Keep the value within the range browsers accept and document the chosen period beside the allow-list.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the token and does not predict the default a particular browser applies when the attribute is discarded.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Max-Age value is not a run of digits.
fp: A negative value is reported too; the rule does not compute the effective cache lifetime.
recordDesc: A non-numeric Access-Control-Max-Age is discarded, so the preflight cache lifetime is whatever the browser defaults to rather than the period the deployment set.
applicability: Preflight responses that send Access-Control-Max-Age.
risk: Preflights are re-issued more often than the deployment expects, which adds load and latency and hides the intended caching policy; LOW because no access decision changes.
why: Access-Control-Max-Age has a non-numeric value.
fix: Write Access-Control-Max-Age as decimal seconds.
Keep the value in the range browsers accept.
verifyT: Send a preflight and confirm Access-Control-Max-Age is a decimal integer.

title: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials carries an unrecognised token
description: The Access-Control-Allow-Credentials value is neither `true` nor `false`: it is some other token such as `1`, `yes` or a list. The protocol compares the header to the exact token `true`, so the value disables credentialed cross-origin access without saying so, and a header that was meant to enable it silently does nothing.
remediation: Emit exactly `true` when credentialed access is intended and remove the header otherwise. Do not pass the flag through a formatter that can spell it differently.
limitation: One header value. Comparison is case-insensitive like every other header value pattern in this pack, so a capitalised True is not reported even though the protocol is case-sensitive; the rule reports values that are not a true/false spelling at all.
scopeT: One response whose Access-Control-Allow-Credentials value is not the literal token true.
fp: A literal false is not reported, because it is a deliberate denial rather than a malformed grant.
recordDesc: Only the token true enables credentialed CORS; a value such as 1 or yes leaves credentials disabled while the header appears to grant them.
applicability: Responses that send Access-Control-Allow-Credentials.
risk: A credentialed cross-origin client fails authentication against an endpoint that looks configured for it; LOW because the browser denies rather than exposes.
why: The value is present and is neither true nor false.
fix: Emit exactly true for credentialed access.
Remove the header where credentials are not needed.
verifyT: Send a credentialed cross-origin request and confirm the value is the exact token true.

cells.name: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials carries an unrecognised token
cells.safe: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is true, false or absent

title: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy value is not a recognised token
description: The Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy value is none of `require-corp`, `credentialless` or `unsafe-none`. A browser discards a value it does not recognise and behaves as if the header were absent, so a deployment that believes it enabled cross-origin isolation is not isolated at all.
remediation: Set Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy to `require-corp` (or `credentialless` where that is the deliberate choice). Check the spelling against the specification rather than a framework default.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the token and does not decide whether the page actually needs isolation or whether its subresources would satisfy require-corp.
scopeT: One response whose Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy value is not a defined token.
fp: A deliberate unsafe-none is not reported here; it has its own rule and its own meaning.
recordDesc: An unrecognised Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy token is ignored, so cross-origin isolation is not enabled even though the header is present.
applicability: Responses that send Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy.
risk: Shared-array buffers and other isolation-dependent features fail, and any protection the operator believed the header added is absent; LOW because the failure is closed rather than open.
why: The value is present and is not one of the three defined tokens.
fix: Set require-corp or credentialless.
Check the value against the specification token list.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm the value is exactly require-corp or credentialless.

title: Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy value is not a recognised token
description: The Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy value is none of `same-origin`, `same-site` or `cross-origin`. A browser ignores an unrecognised token, so the resource is treated as if no policy were declared and can be embedded more widely than the deployment intended.
remediation: Set Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy to one of the three defined tokens and verify the spelling. Use `same-origin` for resources that should never be embedded cross-origin.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the token and does not observe whether any other origin actually embeds the resource.
scopeT: One response whose Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy value is not a defined token.
fp: The token is validated as written; no claim is made about which origin would embed the resource.
recordDesc: An unrecognised Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy token is discarded, so the response falls back to the browser default instead of the declared embedding policy.
applicability: Responses that send Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy.
risk: Another origin embeds the resource in a way the deployment meant to block; LOW because the browser default still applies and the resource must be reachable.
why: The value is present and is not one of the three defined tokens.
fix: Use same-origin, same-site or cross-origin.
Verify the spelling against the token list.
verifyT: Fetch the resource and confirm the value is one of the three tokens.

title: X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies value is not a recognised token
description: The X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies value is none of the five defined tokens (`none`, `master-only`, `by-content-type`, `by-ftp-filename`, `all`). A client that does not recognise the token falls back to its default, so the header states a policy that is not the policy in force.
remediation: Use one of the five defined tokens, normally `none`. Remove values invented by a framework or copied from an unrelated deployment.
limitation: One header value. The rule validates the token and does not inspect whether a cross-domain policy file is actually served.
scopeT: One response whose X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies value is not a defined token.
fp: The presence of a policy file is not checked; only the declared token is judged.
recordDesc: An unrecognised X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies token is ignored, so the declared restriction on cross-domain policy files is not applied as written.
applicability: Responses that send X-Permitted-Cross-Domain-Policies.
risk: A legacy client may load a cross-domain policy the deployment meant to forbid, or refuse one it meant to allow; LOW because the affected clients are legacy and the default is usually restrictive.
why: The value is present and is not one of the five defined tokens.
fix: Use none or master-only.
Remove invented values.
verifyT: Fetch the resource and confirm the token is one of the five defined values.

title: Permissions-Policy allow-list is not closed
description: The Permissions-Policy value opens a feature allow-list with `(` and never closes it. The parser cannot attribute the remaining text to a feature, so the declared restrictions after the opening parenthesis are dropped and the policy is not the one the deployment wrote.
remediation: Close every allow-list and separate features with commas, for example `camera=(self), microphone=()`. Validate the header with a parser before shipping a policy change.
limitation: One header value. The rule detects the unclosed parenthesis only; it does not evaluate which feature ends up enabled by the browser default.
scopeT: One response whose Permissions-Policy value contains an opening parenthesis that is never closed.
fp: A policy that closes every list is not reported even when it grants a feature; the grant rules cover that separately.
recordDesc: An unterminated allow-list makes the Permissions-Policy unparsable from that feature onward, so later features fall back to their defaults instead of the declared restriction.
applicability: Responses that send Permissions-Policy.
risk: A browser grants or denies a feature by default rather than by the written policy, which can enable a feature the deployment meant to restrict; LOW because the malformed text is usually caught in testing.
why: An opening parenthesis in the value has no matching closing parenthesis.
fix: Close every allow-list.
Validate the header with a parser before shipping.
verifyT: Fetch the page and confirm every ( has a matching ).

title: Location header names a script or data scheme
description: The Location header names a `javascript:`, `vbscript:` or `data:` URL instead of a web address. A redirect to such a scheme hands the navigation target to a script or to inline document content, and the response that carries it is indistinguishable from an ordinary redirect until the scheme is read.
remediation: Restrict Location to absolute https URLs or to paths on the same host, and reject any value whose scheme is not http or https before sending it. Never reflect a request parameter into Location without that check.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the scheme the header names; it cannot prove the value is attacker-influenced, and browsers differ in how they treat script schemes in a redirect.
scopeT: One response whose Location value begins with a script or data scheme.
fp: The rule judges the declared scheme only; a redirect to an attacker host over https is a different finding with its own rule.
recordDesc: A Location value with a script or data scheme turns a redirect into script execution or inline document rendering in the redirecting origin context.
applicability: Responses with a Location header.
risk: A response that reflects a request value into Location can be steered to javascript: or data:, which turns an open redirect into script execution; MEDIUM because the reflection must exist.
why: The Location value begins with javascript:, vbscript: or data:.
fix: Allow only http and https targets in Location.
Reject any reflected value whose scheme is not http or https.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and confirm Location never carries a script or data scheme, including with a crafted parameter.

cells.name: Location names a non-navigable scheme
cells.safe: Location names an http or https URL

title: Refresh header targets a data: URL
description: The Refresh header tells the browser to navigate to a `data:` URL. The target is an inline document rather than a web address, so the navigation renders attacker-authored markup under a page transition the user reads as a normal redirect.
remediation: Restrict Refresh to absolute https URLs on hosts you operate, and prefer a server-side redirect with a validated Location. Reject data: and script schemes before emitting the header.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the scheme the header names; it cannot prove the value is attacker-influenced, and some browsers block top-level data: navigation outright.
scopeT: One response whose refresh target begins with the data: scheme.
fp: Blocked or ignored navigations are not distinguished; the finding is the declared target.
recordDesc: A data: target in Refresh renders inline attacker-authored document content after a timed navigation the user did not clearly request.
applicability: Responses with a Refresh header.
risk: A page that reflects a parameter into Refresh can be steered to a data: document that renders a credential prompt in place of the expected page; MEDIUM because the reflection must exist.
why: The Refresh target begins with data:.
fix: Allow only https targets in Refresh.
Prefer a validated Location redirect.
verifyT: Request the endpoint and confirm Refresh never carries a data target.

title: Link header names a script or data URL
description: A Link header target uses `javascript:` or `data:` rather than a web address. Resource hints that name such a scheme make the browser treat inline content as a preloadable or prerenderable resource, and the header carries no origin a policy can pin.
remediation: Emit Link targets as absolute https URLs on hosts you operate, and drop any hint whose target is not a web address. Resource hints should never name a data or script scheme.
limitation: One header value. The rule reports the scheme in the Link target; it does not prove the browser acted on the hint or that the target is attacker-controlled.
scopeT: One response whose Link header contains a target beginning with a script or data scheme.
fp: The rule reads the target scheme only; whether the resource was actually fetched is not observable.
recordDesc: A Link target with a script or data scheme asks the browser to treat inline content as a resource hint target, which no origin allow-list can scope.
applicability: Responses with a Link header.
risk: A prerender or preload of inline attacker-authored content runs ahead of user intent; LOW because browsers gate most such hints and the value must still reach the header.
why: A Link target begins with javascript: or data:.
fix: Emit only https Link targets.
Drop hints that name a non-web scheme.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm every Link target is an https URL.

title: Kubernetes API server version endpoint disclosed
description: The response is the Kubernetes API server version document: a JSON object carrying gitVersion, platform and build metadata. That endpoint is part of the cluster control-plane API, so an unauthenticated caller reached the API surface rather than an application page.
remediation: Restrict the Kubernetes API server to the control-plane network and to authenticated callers, and do not publish it through the same ingress as the application. Anonymous access to /version is disabled by default in supported releases; re-check the API server flags if it is enabled.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the version document, which proves the API surface answered; it does not prove that cluster objects are readable without credentials, and the version alone is not a vulnerability.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both a gitVersion field and a platform field.
fp: A hardened API server that returns the same document to an authenticated operator is not a finding; the rule reports reachability of the endpoint, not who may call it.
recordDesc: The Kubernetes API server answers the version endpoint and returns its build metadata, which means the control-plane API is reachable from this network position and reports its exact version.
applicability: Responses whose body is served from a Kubernetes control-plane endpoint.
risk: A caller who can read the API version can match it to known issues for that release and confirm the cluster API is reachable; LOW because the document carries version metadata rather than cluster objects.
why: The body is the API server version document with gitVersion and platform fields.
fix: Close anonymous access to the API server.
Confirm the version endpoint is unreachable from untrusted networks.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the version document is not returned to unauthenticated callers.

title: Kubernetes Dashboard interface disclosed
description: The response is the Kubernetes Dashboard single-page application: its bundle names and root element appear in the markup. The dashboard is a cluster management interface, so its presence identifies an administrative console on the network.
remediation: Keep the dashboard on an internal network behind an authenticating proxy, or remove it where it is not required. Do not publish it through the same ingress as application traffic.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the dashboard front end; it does not prove that the login can be bypassed or that a service account token is reachable.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both the dashboard bundle name and the Kubernetes Dashboard title.
fp: A dashboard deliberately published to an authenticated internal audience is still reported; the finding is reachability, not proof of a bypass.
recordDesc: The Kubernetes Dashboard front end is served at this endpoint, so the cluster administration interface is reachable and its login flow is exposed to whoever can reach this host.
applicability: Responses served by a Kubernetes Dashboard deployment.
risk: An attacker who reaches the dashboard can attempt its authentication flow against a cluster-admin surface; MEDIUM because the page itself does not prove that credentials are accepted.
why: The body carries the dashboard bundle and the Kubernetes Dashboard title.
fix: Move the dashboard behind an authenticating proxy.
Confirm the page is unreachable from untrusted networks.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the dashboard front end is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Kubelet pod list disclosed
description: The response is a Kubernetes PodList document: the kubelet read-only API returns the pods scheduled on the node, including namespaces and container images. That endpoint normally answers only on the node network or to authenticated callers.
remediation: Disable the kubelet read-only port or set authentication and authorization on the kubelet, and restrict the node network. Anonymous access to the kubelet API is not a supported configuration.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the pod list the kubelet returned; it does not attempt any other kubelet endpoint and cannot show whether exec or logs are reachable.
scopeT: One response whose body is a PodList document with apiVersion and items fields.
fp: A cluster that deliberately serves the pod list to a monitoring system on a trusted network is still reported; the finding is the reachable endpoint.
recordDesc: The kubelet API returned its pod list, so the node-level API is reachable and discloses workload names, namespaces and image identities.
applicability: Responses served by a kubelet API endpoint.
risk: Workload names, namespaces and image tags map the cluster and identify versions to target; HIGH because the kubelet API also exposes other read endpoints when it is reachable in this mode.
why: The body is a PodList document with apiVersion, items and pod metadata.
fix: Disable anonymous kubelet access.
Confirm the pod list is not returned without credentials.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the pod list is not returned to an unauthenticated caller.

title: Grafana interface disclosed
description: The response is the Grafana front end: the page inlines grafanaBootData with the build information used to bootstrap the application. Grafana is a dashboarding product that often holds data-source credentials and query access to production metrics.
remediation: Keep Grafana on an internal network behind an authenticating proxy, disable anonymous access, and do not expose it through the application ingress.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the Grafana shell; it does not prove that a dashboard or data source is readable without credentials.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both grafanaBootData and a buildInfo object.
fp: A Grafana instance published to a deliberate audience is still reported; the finding is the exposed console, not a proven data read.
recordDesc: The Grafana application shell is served at this endpoint with its boot data, so the dashboarding console is reachable and reports its build version.
applicability: Responses served by a Grafana deployment.
risk: A reachable Grafana instance exposes its login flow, provisioning defaults and any anonymous-access configuration; MEDIUM because the page alone does not prove that data sources are readable.
why: The body carries grafanaBootData and a buildInfo object.
fix: Restrict Grafana to the internal network.
Confirm anonymous access is disabled and the page is unreachable.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the Grafana shell is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Kibana interface disclosed

remediation: Keep Kibana on an internal network behind an authenticating proxy and disable anonymous access. Do not publish it through the application ingress.

applicability: Responses served by a Kibana deployment.

title: Jupyter notebook server disclosed
description: The response is the Jupyter Notebook tree page: the title and the notebook_path attribute identify the server that lists notebooks and kernels. A notebook server exposes a file browser and a kernel that executes code.
remediation: Require the server token on every interface, bind the server to loopback, and place it behind an authenticating proxy. Never expose the notebook server on an application ingress.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the tree page; it does not attempt to start a kernel or read a notebook, and a token-protected server is indistinguishable from an open one at this layer.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both the Jupyter Notebook title and a notebook_path attribute.
fp: A deliberately published notebook server is still reported; the finding is reachability, not proof that a kernel can be started.
recordDesc: The Jupyter Notebook server answered with its tree page, so the notebook file browser and kernel API are reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by a Jupyter notebook server.
risk: A reachable notebook server can list files and start kernels that execute code under the service account; HIGH because kernel execution is arbitrary code by design when the token gate is absent.
why: The body carries the Jupyter Notebook title and a notebook_path attribute.
fix: Require the server token and bind to loopback.
Confirm the tree page is not returned without a token.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the tree page is refused without the server token.

Confirm authentication is enabled and the page is unreachable.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the Airflow page is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Zabbix interface disclosed
description: The response is the Zabbix front end: the zabbix bundle and the product attribution identify the monitoring console. Zabbix holds host inventories, agent credentials and alerting integrations.
remediation: Keep Zabbix on an internal network behind an authenticating proxy, require authentication, and keep the front end patched.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the Zabbix shell; it does not read a host or a trigger.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both the zabbix bundle and the product name.
fp: A deliberately published instance is still reported; the finding is reachability.
recordDesc: The Zabbix console is served at this endpoint, so the monitoring interface, with its host inventory and alert history, is reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by a Zabbix front end.
risk: A reachable monitoring console exposes host inventory and trigger history after login and is a frequent target for its own known issues; MEDIUM because the page alone does not prove access.
why: The body carries the zabbix bundle and the product name.
fix: Restrict the console to the internal network.
Confirm the page is unreachable from untrusted callers.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the Zabbix page is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Jaeger tracing UI disclosed
description: The response is the Jaeger query UI: the jaeger-ui bundle and the product name identify the tracing console. Traces carry service names, timings and sometimes request attributes from production traffic.
remediation: Keep the Jaeger query service on an internal network behind an authenticating proxy and restrict trace retention to what is needed.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the UI shell; it does not fetch a trace and cannot show which attributes a span carries.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both the jaeger-ui bundle and the product name.
fp: A deliberately published tracing UI is still reported; the finding is reachability.
recordDesc: The Jaeger query interface is served at this endpoint, so the tracing console with its stored spans is reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by a Jaeger query service.
risk: A reachable tracing console exposes service maps, operation names and sampled request attributes; MEDIUM because the page alone does not prove that traces are readable.
why: The body carries the jaeger-ui bundle and the Jaeger product name.
fix: Restrict the query service to the internal network.
Confirm the UI is unreachable from untrusted callers.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the Jaeger UI is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Azure Blob Storage container listing disclosed
description: The response is an Azure Blob Storage container listing: the EnumerationResults document with BlobService metadata returns blob names to an anonymous caller. The container was reached without a shared access signature.
remediation: Set the container access level to private and serve public assets through a controlled endpoint or a signed URL. Review the container policy for anonymous read.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the listing document; it does not download a blob and cannot show what the blobs contain.
scopeT: One response whose body is an Azure container listing with an EnumerationResults root and BlobService metadata.
fp: A container deliberately configured for public read is still reported; the finding is that anonymous listing is enabled, not that the data is sensitive.
recordDesc: The blob container answered with an EnumerationResults document, so anonymous listing is enabled on a container that this caller could reach.
applicability: Anonymous responses from an Azure Blob Storage container endpoint.
risk: Blob names reveal backup schedules, customer identifiers and file layouts, and a readable blob can be downloaded directly; MEDIUM because the listing itself is metadata and the container may hold only public assets.
why: The body is an EnumerationResults document with a BlobService marker.
fix: Set the container access level to private.
Confirm anonymous listing returns an authorization error.
verifyT: Request the container URL without credentials and confirm the listing is refused.

title: Cloud Storage bucket listing disclosed
description: The response is a Cloud Storage bucket listing served through the XML API: the ListBucketResult document and the storage.googleapis.com marker identify the bucket and return object keys to an anonymous caller.
remediation: Remove the allUsers storage.objects.list grant, keep the bucket private, and serve public assets through a controlled endpoint or a signed URL.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the listing; it does not download an object and cannot show what the objects contain.
scopeT: One response whose body is a bucket listing with a ListBucketResult root served from storage.googleapis.com.
fp: A bucket deliberately configured for public listing is still reported; the finding is the anonymous listing, not that the objects are sensitive.
recordDesc: The bucket answered with an object listing, so anonymous list permission is granted to allUsers on a bucket that this caller could reach.
applicability: Anonymous responses from a Cloud Storage bucket XML endpoint.
risk: Object keys reveal backup names, tenant identifiers and file layouts, and a readable object can be downloaded directly; MEDIUM because the listing is metadata and the bucket may hold public assets only.
why: The body is a ListBucketResult document from a Cloud Storage endpoint.
fix: Remove the allUsers list grant.
Confirm anonymous listing returns an authorization error.
verifyT: Request the bucket URL without credentials and confirm the listing is refused.

title: CouchDB HTTP API root disclosed
description: The response is the CouchDB HTTP API root document: the couchdb Welcome field and the version field identify an unauthenticated CouchDB server. That API exposes databases and documents directly.
remediation: Require the admin credentials, create named users, bind the interface to the internal network, and keep the version patched.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the root document; it does not enumerate a database or read a document.
scopeT: One response whose body is a CouchDB welcome document with couchdb and version fields.
fp: A deliberately public CouchDB root is still reported; the finding is the reachable API, not a proven document read.
recordDesc: The CouchDB API root answered with its welcome document, so the database HTTP interface is reachable and reports its version.
applicability: Responses from a CouchDB HTTP API endpoint.
risk: A reachable CouchDB API exposes database names and documents when the admin party is open, which is still the default in some deployments; MEDIUM because the root document alone does not prove document access.
why: The body carries the couchdb Welcome field and a version field.
fix: Require an admin and named users.
Confirm the root document is refused without credentials.
verifyT: Request the API root without credentials and confirm it does not return the welcome document.

title: Apache Solr admin interface disclosed
description: The response is the Solr administration interface: the solr-spec-version and lucene-spec-version fields identify the search server and its exact library versions. Solr admin exposes cores, schemas and query endpoints.
remediation: Keep the Solr admin interface on the management network or behind an authenticating proxy, disable the admin UI where it is not needed, and keep the version patched.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the admin page; it does not run a query or read a core.
scopeT: One response whose body contains both solr-spec-version and lucene-spec-version fields.
fp: A deliberately published admin interface is still reported; the finding is reachability.
recordDesc: The Solr administration interface is served at this endpoint, so the search server console is reachable and reports its versions.
applicability: Responses served by a Solr administration interface.
risk: A reachable Solr admin exposes core configuration and query endpoints and identifies the exact version to target; MEDIUM because the page alone does not prove that a core is readable.
why: The body carries solr-spec-version and lucene-spec-version fields.
fix: Restrict the admin interface to the management network.
Confirm the page is unreachable from untrusted callers.
verifyT: Fetch the endpoint and confirm the Solr admin page is not served to untrusted callers.

title: ZooKeeper stat command output disclosed
description: The response is ZooKeeper four-letter command output: the version banner with the latency and node counters is what the stat command returns. The four-letter commands are an unauthenticated administrative surface when they are enabled.
remediation: Disable the four-letter commands with the whitelist configuration, or restrict them to the management network. Keep the client port off untrusted networks.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the stat output; it does not attempt a write command and cannot show whether one is enabled.
scopeT: One response whose body carries a ZooKeeper version banner and the stat latency counters.
fp: A deliberately restricted stat response is still reported; the finding is that the command surface answered, not that a write is possible.
recordDesc: ZooKeeper answered a four-letter command with its stat output, so the administrative command surface is reachable and reports version, connection and node counts.
applicability: Responses from a ZooKeeper client port that accepts four-letter commands.
risk: An attacker who reaches the four-letter surface can read server state and, when the write commands are enabled, shut the ensemble down; MEDIUM because the stat output itself is metadata.
why: The body carries the ZooKeeper version banner and the latency counters of the stat command.
fix: Disable the four-letter commands.
Confirm the command surface refuses unauthenticated callers.
verifyT: Send a four-letter command and confirm it is refused or restricted to the management network.

title: Docker daemon API info disclosed
description: The response is the Docker daemon info document: DockerRootDir, ApiVersion and ServerVersion are fields of the /info endpoint. That endpoint belongs to the daemon API, which can create and run containers.
remediation: Never expose the Docker daemon TCP socket. Bind it to a local socket, and if remote access is required put an authenticating TLS proxy in front of it with client certificates.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the info document; it does not list a container or start one, so it does not prove that container control is possible from this position.
scopeT: One response whose body is a Docker info document with DockerRootDir and ApiVersion fields.
fp: A daemon behind a mutually authenticated proxy that still returns info to an authorised caller is not a finding; the rule reports reachability from this position.
recordDesc: The Docker daemon API answered its info endpoint, so the container runtime control plane is reachable and reports host and version details.
applicability: Responses from a Docker daemon API endpoint.
risk: A caller who reaches the daemon API can list containers and, where the socket is exposed without a proxy, start one with host mounts; HIGH because the API is root-equivalent on the host.
why: The body is a Docker info document with DockerRootDir and ApiVersion fields.
fix: Stop exposing the daemon TCP socket.
Confirm the API is reachable only over a local socket or a mutually authenticated proxy.
verifyT: Request the info endpoint and confirm the daemon API is not reachable without mutual TLS.

title: Apache Spark master UI disclosed
description: The response is the Spark master web UI: the Spark Master heading with the spark:// URL identifies the cluster manager and its coordinator address. The UI lists applications, workers and drivers.
remediation: Keep the Spark master UI on the internal network and enable the authentication filter. Do not publish port 8080 through the application ingress.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the master UI; it does not submit an application and cannot show whether submission is open.
scopeT: One response whose body carries the Spark Master heading and a spark:// coordinator URL.
fp: A deliberately published UI is still reported; the finding is reachability.
recordDesc: The Spark master UI is served at this endpoint, so the cluster coordinator and its application list are reachable from this network position.
applicability: Responses served by a Spark master web UI.
risk: The UI exposes application names, worker hosts and driver logs, which map the cluster and its data pipelines; MEDIUM because the page is read-only.
why: The body carries the Spark Master heading and a spark:// coordinator URL.
fix: Restrict the master UI to the internal network.
Confirm the UI is unreachable from untrusted callers.
verifyT: Fetch the master UI and confirm it is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Hadoop NameNode UI disclosed
description: The response is the Hadoop NameNode web UI: the NameNode heading with an hdfs:// address identifies the filesystem coordinator. The UI lists live data nodes, capacity and block information.
remediation: Keep the NameNode UI on the internal network behind an authenticating proxy and enable the Hadoop HTTP authentication setting where the UI must be reachable.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the NameNode UI; it does not browse the filesystem and cannot show whether file access is open.
scopeT: One response whose body carries the NameNode heading and an hdfs:// address.
fp: A deliberately published UI is still reported; the finding is reachability.
recordDesc: The NameNode UI is served at this endpoint, so the Hadoop filesystem coordinator is reachable and reports its cluster address.
applicability: Responses served by a Hadoop NameNode web UI.
risk: The UI exposes data-node hosts, capacity and block counts that map the storage cluster; MEDIUM because the page is read-only and no file content is returned.
why: The body carries the NameNode heading and an hdfs:// address.
fix: Restrict the UI to the internal network.
Confirm the page is unreachable from untrusted callers.
verifyT: Fetch the NameNode UI and confirm it is not served to untrusted callers.

title: Spring Actuator health details disclosed
description: The response is the Spring Boot Actuator health document with component details: the status field and the diskSpace component show that health detail is published rather than summarised. The detail names the storage paths, database product and free capacity.
remediation: Set management.endpoint.health.show-details to never or to when-authorized, and keep the management port on the internal network rather than the application port.
limitation: One response body. The rule reports the health detail; it does not call another actuator endpoint and cannot show whether env or heapdump is exposed.
scopeT: One response whose body is a health document with a status field and a diskSpace component.
fp: A health document with a diskSpace component served to an authorised operator is still reported; the finding is that detail is published, not who may read it.
recordDesc: The Actuator health endpoint returned component detail, so the management surface is reachable and reports internal component names and storage paths.
applicability: Responses served by a Spring Boot Actuator health endpoint.
risk: The detail discloses the database product and filesystem paths and gives capacity headroom for a storage-exhaustion attempt; LOW because the document carries no credentials or business data.
why: The body is an Actuator health document with a status field and a diskSpace component.
fix: Set show-details to never or when-authorized.
Confirm the health endpoint returns a summary only.
verifyT: Request the health endpoint and confirm it returns a status summary without component detail.
